newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Denmark to press ahead on China rights resolution.
newsitem.headline: Denmark to press ahead on China rights resolution.

text.p: Denmark said on Monday it was pressing ahead with a U.N. resolution criticising China's human rights record despite French objections and a warning from Beijing that it would severely damage relations.
Denmark plans to table the controversial resolution this week at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva after European Union discord thwarted attempts to agree a joint EU motion.
"We have made our decision," Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen told the Danish Ritzaus news agency.

Despite Danish resolve and the backing of most EU countries this year, Western efforts to have a resolution passed on China's rights performance have failed since Beijing's bloody crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in 1989. China has rallied enough support each time to block the move.

The sensitive issue of a resolution condemning China was debated by EU foreign ministers during a meeting in the Dutch coastal town of Noordwijk. The Netherlands, current holder of the rotating EU presidency, had been expected to present the annual EU-sponsored resolution on behalf of all 15 members.
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo said most EU countries supported the Danish-led resolution criticising China's human rights record.
In Beijing, China warned Denmark that relations would be severely damaged if it pressed ahead,
"If Denmark insists on doing this it will end up as the biggest loser," said Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang.
The failure to agree a joint resolution has sparked concerns about the EU's credibility on the world stage at a time when it seeks to strengthen its common foreign and security policy.

Denmark decided to move after France declared last month that dialogue with China was better than confrontation, refusing to support the joint EU-motion. Germany, Spain and Italy had since adopted a similar position, diplomats said.
But while France continued to oppose it, most other EU countries signalled their support for the Danish-sponsored resolution, which has also won firm U.S. backing.
"The Danes already have the support of 11, perhaps 12, (countries)," van Mierlo told reporters.
Swedish Foreign Minister Lena Hjelm-Wallen said there would probably be four EU countries which would not support the resolution on China.
Van Mierlo warned of applying double standards on human rights, to take a different approach towards large countries like China and smaller nations which are not as commercially important.
"There is the risk of double standards by the EU towards big powerful countries and smaller, not powerful, countries," he said. "This is not compatible with the universality of human rights."
Sweden's Hjelm-Wallebn took a similar line, saying human rights are "absolute".
Last week, van Mierlo warned that the failure to agree on the China motion was a serious setback for prospects of a common EU foreign policy.
The United States welcomed Denmark's decision and offered to co-sponsor the resolution.
"This decision by Denmark reflects its principled commitment to the universality of human rights," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in a statement on Saturday.
In Geneva on Sunday, diplomats said China had launched a rearguard action at the U.N. Human Rights Commission to head off the resolution condemning it for abusing human rights.
They said China was actively lobbying other countries to block the Danish resolution and that it might succeed again.

The wording of the resolution had not yet been released but Petersen told Ritzau news agency that China should be criticised for its lack of respect for basic human rights such as freedom of assembly and speech.
